title: Answering questions
hookLine: saying I don't know is half of knowledge (reported from early scholars)
tomorrow: Amira's roommate is curious. how much do you share?

lines: I DON'T KNOW. I DON'T KNOW.
cards: Someone at work asks a question, and the answer is halfway out of your mouth before you notice you don't actually know it. Ever done that? Here's a man who wouldn't.
Medina. A traveler has come a long way with a list of questions for Imam Malik, the scholar people journeyed to the city to ask. He asks the first.
Malik says: I don't know. He asks another. I don't know.
Question after question, the same two words. Finally, tradition says, the traveler bursts out: I came all this way. What am I supposed to tell the people back home?

teach.b: And Malik answers: tell them Malik says, I don't know. That's the whole reply, and it's the point.
A saying reported from early scholars puts it plainly: I don't know is half of knowledge. Half, because everything you do know is only safe standing next to it.

The Qur'an gives the angels the same words. When God asks them to name what they were never taught, they say, in Pickthall's words: "Be glorified! We have no knowledge saving that which Thou hast taught us."
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said it too.

In the hadith of Jibril, a stranger questions him in front of his companions, and when he's asked when the Hour will come, he answers that the one being asked knows no more about it than the one asking.
A teacher, naming a limit, with everyone watching. The Qur'an turns it into a rule: "follow not that whereof thou hast no knowledge."
So I don't know isn't where a teacher fails. Said honestly, and followed by let's find out, it keeps what gets passed on clean.
One to tell a friend tonight: the scholar people traveled to Medina to ask is remembered for two small words.

how: When a question is beyond them, Muslim teachers and students may say 'Allahu a'lam', God knows best, or 'la adri', I don't know, and pass the question on to someone who knows.

o: always having a ready answer for any question
repeating what the teacher said, word for word
answering what you know, and admitting where it stops

games.q: who said it — tap the pairs.
p: tell them Malik says I don't know
no knowledge but what You taught us
the asked knows no more than the asker
follow not what you don't know

s: a good teacher always has an answer ready
tradition remembers Imam Malik for saying I don't know, and the Prophet named a limit in the hadith of Jibril.
in the Qur'an, the angels admit what they don't know
2:32: we have no knowledge saving that which Thou hast taught us.
'I don't know is half of knowledge' is a verse of the Qur'an
it's a saying reported from early scholars, not a verse.

games.q: a coworker asks you if layoffs are coming. you've heard rumors, nothing official, and she looks worried. what fits Malik's two words?
o: pass on the rumor, so at least she can get ready.
say I don't know, and point her to someone who would.
tell her no, so she can stop worrying for now.
games.why: Malik wouldn't send a traveler home with a guess, and 17:36 says not to follow what you don't know. an honest limit plus a next step is the kind answer.

practice: Bring to mind one question you've been half-answering: from a kid, a friend, a coworker, or yourself. Say out loud, quietly: I don't know. Then: let's find out.
Sit with those two lines until the time is up, and let the quiet after them stay quiet.

wordCard.voice: Answering questions: saying what you know, and saying I don't know where it stops. Malik's two words, and the angels'.

orig.note: Arabic: I don't know. The reply tradition remembers from Imam Malik.

carryVoice: Your line: I don't know. Two honest words keep the door to the answer open. Six of ten for passing it on.
